{
  "question": "What has been proposed to reduce the risk of AI systems making unreliable judgments in unfamiliar situations or for different people, and by what mechanism?",
  "reference_answer": "The proposal is to make programmers more aware of the human judgments they implicitly build into AI systems and of those judgments’ limitations. Selecting training examples and deciding whether a classifier performs acceptably already injects programmers’ judgments, supported by their human empathy and prediction capacities. These capacities differ between people and work reliably only in typical circumstances, so systems trained through them may not transfer reliably to new situations or other people. Programmers should therefore recognize these hidden dependencies and check whether their application involves substantially divergent judgments, rather than treating their modeling choices as universally valid facts. This awareness is proposed to improve generalization by making the sources and limits of the training judgments visible; no specific technical procedure or guarantee is supplied.",
  "spans": [
    "The programmers are using their own E and P modules to establish that certain articles are a) likely to be clicked on, but b) not what the clicker would really want to read. So the whole process is entirely dependent on programmer judgement - it might feel like \"debugging\", or \"making reasonable modelling choices\", but its actually injecting the programmers' judgements into the system.",
    "But there are two caveats: first, not everyone will agree, because there is not perfect agreement between the empathy modules. The programmers should be careful as to whether this is an area of very divergent judgements or not.",
    "And second, these results will likely not generalise well to new distributions. That's because having *implicit* access to categorisation modules that themselves are valid only in typical situations... is not a way to generalise well. At all.",
    "Hence we should expect poor generalisation from such methods, to other situations and (sometimes) to other humans.",
    "In my opinion, **if programmers are more aware of these issues, they will have better generalisation performance**."
  ]
}
